# [[1.0.0 P-116 — Gauthier 2024-2025 — Aider: AI Pair Programming in Your Terminal]]

- **Authors**: Paul Gauthier (Aider AI; independent / open-source maintainer).
- **Venue / Year**: [INFERENCE: practitioner tech-report; not formally peer-reviewed]. Aider is documented as a continuously-maintained open-source project (https://aider.chat and the https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider repository) accompanied by blog posts, the `aider-docs/` technical reference, the Aider polyglot benchmark write-up, and an evolving set of LLM-eval leaderboards. There is no single canonical peer-reviewed paper; the citation typically used is "Gauthier, P., 2024. Aider: AI Pair Programming in Your Terminal. https://aider.chat" or the GitHub release tags / arXiv-style write-ups posted at https://aider.chat (the most-cited authoritative artefact is the `aider.chat/2024/01` and `aider.chat/2024/08` design write-ups plus the December 2024 polyglot benchmark report). Year attribution is 2024 for the initial chat-with-repo design and 2025 for the polyglot / LLM-eval-leaderboard era; both are correct depending on the cited artefact. Verify against `aider.chat/docs/` and the GitHub release history before quoting as definitive.
- **URL**: https://aider.chat ; https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider ; benchmark dashboards at https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/ ; polyglot benchmark write-up at https://aider.chat/2024/12/21/aider-polyglot.html (or successor URL).
- **Anchors**: PRIM-9 (Tri-Representation Hybrid Code Graph), PRIM-22 (Four Phases of Comprehension), PRIM-26 (Symbol-Aware Navigator), PRIM-31 (Iterative Retrieval Refinement); the **canonical repo-map + diff-based terminal coding assistant** and the most widely-targeted LLM/SLM benchmark substrate for "edit-the-file" tasks outside SWE-bench.

## 1. Core Contribution

Aider is a **terminal-resident AI pair-programming assistant** that operates on a local checkout of a repository and produces **structured unified-diff edits** against the repository files. The system is the most widely-cited practitioner baseline for "LLM coding at the terminal" and has, since 2024, become a **benchmark substrate in its own right** (the Aider polyglot benchmark). The contribution decomposes into four elements:

1. **Repository map (the structural-context substrate).** Before any edit, Aider builds a **repo-map**: a tree-sitter-parsed AST-derived digest of every file in the repo, listing each top-level class / function / method with its signature, line number, and call-graph-adjacent neighbours. The repo-map is the **initial system prompt** the LM sees; it is the structural context that tells the model "this is the shape of the codebase" without forcing the LM to ingest every file. The repo-map is **the per-file AST analogue** that AutoCodeRover's retrieval generalises to multi-representation CPG; it is **the same substrate** [[1.0.0 P-113]] uses internally and the substrate that maps directly to MAgHARCM's PRIM-9 (CPG) + PRIM-26 (symbol-aware navigator).

2. **Whole-file diff as the output primitive.** The agent emits **unified diffs** anchored to the file-level; the diff format is the same one humans write and the same one `git apply` consumes. The host parses the diff, applies it, and re-parses the file with tree-sitter to verify the post-edit AST is still well-formed. This **diff-first** discipline is the conceptual sibling of [[1.0.0 P-113]] AutoCodeRover's minimal-diff output format and the SWE-agent [[1.0.0 P-112]] `edit` ACI; Aider is the system that made "edit = unified diff" the standard for terminal-based coding agents.

3. **Chat-with-repo as an iterative comprehension loop.** Aider maintains a **running conversation** with the LM where each turn contains (a) the latest repo-map (refreshed when files change), (b) the file contents the LM has previously requested via `read` / `cat`-style operations, and (c) the previous diffs. The conversation is the **DR. JONES four-phase comprehension trace** rendered as a chat transcript: each turn Search → Anchoring → Reasoning → Recertification maps onto a `read some file` → `propose diff` → `apply diff` → `re-run linter/test` micro-cycle. The chat loop is **iterative retrieval refinement** in the sense of [[1.0.0 PRIM-31]]: the model can issue follow-up file fetches, narrow its search, and re-issue a more-precise diff.

4. **The Aider polyglot benchmark as the practitioner evaluation substrate.** Since late 2024, the Aider benchmark (`aider.chat/2024/12/21/aider-polyglot.html` and successor write-ups) has become the **de facto cross-vendor LLM-coding leaderboard**: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, DeepSeek-Coder-V2, Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct, Llama-3.1, and others are ranked on Aider's "edit-the-file" metric. The benchmark is **complementary to** [[1.0.0 P-111]] SWE-bench (which tests whole-repository issue resolution) and **contrasted with** HumanEval (which tests single-function synthesis); Aider is the **per-file edit benchmark** that fills the gap between them. The polyglot benchmark's role as an LLM/SLM scoring substrate is part of the contribution: Aider is not only a coding assistant, it is **the harness that vendors use to grade their models**.

**Headline empirical findings** (paraphrased from the Aider blog and leaderboards, marked `[INFERENCE: verify against current leaderboard before quoting exact numbers]`):
- Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Anthropic) leads the polyglot benchmark for most of 2024–2025 with pass-rates in the **~85–95%** range depending on the variant and the polyglot edition; the Aider maintainer's blog reports Sonnet as the "best of breed" for diff-based editing.
- GPT-4o (OpenAI) lands in the **~70–85%** range on the same benchmark, depending on the prompt-mode setting ("architect" vs "diff-fenced" vs "whole").
- DeepSeek-Coder-V2 (MoE, 236B-A21B) is the **open-weights frontier** that competes with the proprietary frontier on Aider; it lands in the **~75–85%** range depending on the benchmark edition.
- The Aider benchmark **explicitly does not** measure SWE-bench-style issue resolution; the two benchmarks are complementary and measure different scaffolds.
- Pass-rate numbers **vary materially** with the prompt mode (chat vs "architect" decomposition), the model temperature, the repository context size, and whether the model is allowed to issue follow-up `read` operations; Aider is the most thoroughly-ablated practitioner benchmark.

**Why Aider matters for the SLM regime**: Aider is the **per-file-edit benchmark** that the 4B–30B SLM regime can actually be evaluated on. SWE-bench Verified requires a 75-step agent loop with multi-tool retrieval; Aider polyglot requires a single-turn or two-turn `read → diff` interaction. The narrow output space (`unified diff`) and the structural context substrate (`repo-map`) make Aider **the most SLM-friendly practitioner benchmark** — and the benchmark whose scaffold philosophy (structural context + narrow diff output) most closely matches MAgHARCM's composition of PRIM-9, PRIM-22, PRIM-26, PRIM-31.

## 2. Application in MAgHARCM

Aider anchors four primitives in MAgHARCM's agent design. It is not just a paper MAgHARCM cites — it is the **practitioner substrate** whose repo-map + diff pattern MAgHARCM re-implements in Go with the 4B–30B SLM regime in mind, and the **benchmark harness** against which MAgHARCM's per-file-edit primitive outputs are scored.

### 2.1 PRIM-9 (Tri-Representation Hybrid Code Graph)

PRIM-9 (`internal/agents/cpg.go::BuildCPG`) assembles a **Code Property Graph** (AST ∪ CFG ∪ DFG, lifted to inter-procedural scope as a System Dependence Graph) — the three-representation substrate that Yamaguchi 2014 [[1.0.0 P-72]] introduced for vulnerability analysis and that [[1.0.0 P-110]] GraphCoder / CodeGraphRAG elevated to the canonical graph-RAG substrate for code. Aider's **repo-map** is the **single-representation AST leg** of the CPG: tree-sitter parses every file, the AST is flattened into a digest of top-level symbols (class headers, function signatures, method prototypes, field declarations), and the digest is what the LM sees. The mapping:
- **PRIM-9 AST leg ↔ Aider repo-map** — both use tree-sitter as the parser; both treat the AST digest as the canonical structural context; both reject raw file ingestion as the primary mode.
- **PRIM-9 CPG/SDG legs ↔ Aider's "follow-up `read`" protocol** — Aider's chat loop lets the model issue follow-up `read <file>` operations when the repo-map is insufficient; this is **on-demand multi-hop retrieval** without the multi-representation generalisation. PRIM-9's CPG/SDG is the *precomputed, multi-representation* generalisation that lifts Aider's "read this file" follow-up into "walk the CPG/SDG to find the side-effect-relevant symbols".
- **PRIM-9 as Aider's graph-substrate extension** — the empirical claim of MAgHARCM is that *the multi-representation CPG substrate lifts the SLM pass-rate on Aider polyglot by another 5–15 percentage points above the repo-map baseline*. This is the empirical anchor for PRIM-9's existence as the multi-representation generalisation of Aider's repo-map.

### 2.2 PRIM-22 (Four Phases of Comprehension)

Aider's chat loop is the **canonical practitioner rendering** of [[1.0.0 P-40]] DR. JONES' four phases of program comprehension, executed turn by turn:
- **DR. JONES Search ↔ Aider's initial repo-map + `read` queries** — the *search* phase is the repo-map construction at session-start, plus any follow-up `read <path>` operations the LM issues during a turn; the *anchoring* phase is the LM's accumulation of named-symbol evidence in the conversation context.
- **DR. JONES Reasoning ↔ Aider's diff emission** — the *reasoning* phase is the LM's prompt-conditioned diff synthesis; the *recertification* phase is the host's tree-sitter re-parse after diff application (the LM is told "the file is now syntactically valid" or receives a parse error and re-issues a corrected diff).
- **Slot-formatted trace ↔ Aider's "architect" mode** — Aider supports an "architect" mode where the LM first emits a structured plan (a slot-formatted description of which files to touch and why), then emits the diffs. This is the **articulate phase** that PRIM-22 adds on top of AutoCodeRover's five-stage loop: the structured plan is the comprehension trace that downstream agents consume.
- **PRIM-22 as Aider's slot-formatted extension** — MAgHARCM's `internal/agents/comprehension.go` instantiates a six-step DR. JONES variant (Decomposition, Recognition, Organization, Navigation, Explanation, Search) that wraps Aider's repo-map + diff loop with an explicit *Explanation* step — the slot-formatted articulation that PRIM-22 emits for downstream agents and for the bench-eval harness.

### 2.3 PRIM-26 (Symbol-Aware Navigator)

Aider's repo-map **is** a symbol-aware navigator: every entry in the repo-map is a *named symbol operation* (class name, function signature, method prototype, field declaration), and the LM's chat loop accumulates evidence by querying this navigator through `read <file>:<symbol>` style operations. MAgHARCM's `internal/agents/navigator.go` exposes the same surface (`SearchSymbols`, `GetDefinition`, `GetReferences`, `SearchRepoGraph`) and extends it with:
- **Multi-representation queries** (`SearchRepoGraph(term)` walks CPG/SDG, not just AST) — this is the PRIM-9 contribution to PRIM-26.
- **tree-sitter-driven symbol resolution** — Aider's repo-map is built by tree-sitter; MAgHARCM's navigator uses tree-sitter as the canonical parser and adds abcoder MCP integration (`configs/agents.yml::lsp.provider: abcoder-mcp`) for productionised symbol resolution at repository scale.
- **HyperAgent-style retrieval composition** — MAgHARCM's navigator inherits [[1.0.0 P-13]] HyperAgent's composition patterns for multi-step retrieval, which generalise Aider's flat `read <path>` queries into a typed plan (retrieve callers, then retrieve tests, then retrieve recent edits).

### 2.4 PRIM-31 (Iterative Retrieval Refinement)

Aider's chat loop is **the canonical practitioner instance** of iterative retrieval refinement: the LM issues a query (`read file X`, `read function Y in file Z`), inspects the result, issues a follow-up query (`read the callers of Y`), inspects, and so on, until the diff is precise enough to apply. The chat loop is **the interactive instantiation** of the same iterative-retrieval pattern that [[1.0.0 P-110]] GraphCoder / CodeGraphRAG formalises as a typed retrieval plan and that [[1.0.0 P-113]] AutoCodeRover's Understand → Contextualize → Hypothesize → Verify → Repair cycle executes automatically. The mapping:
- **PRIM-31's iterative retrieval ↔ Aider's chat loop** — both refine the retrieval query based on the previous result; both bound the iteration count (Aider by the chat-token budget, PRIM-31 by a max-retrieval-rounds parameter).
- **PRIM-31 as Aider's typed-plan extension** — MAgHARCM's `internal/agents/retrieval_refiner.go` exposes a typed retrieval-plan API (named queries with typed inputs/outputs) that Aider's free-form `read` operations generalise to; this lets MAgHARCM compose retrieval plans across agents (the comprehension agent emits a retrieval plan, the navigator executes it, the patch synthesiser consumes the result).
- **PRIM-31 as Aider's recertification-extension** — Aider's recertification step is the post-diff tree-sitter re-parse; PRIM-31 generalises this to a **structured recertification plan** that includes test execution, linter checks, and AST validity as separately-reportable signals.

### 2.5 SLM Fleet Inference Cost (cross-primitive summary)

Aider's design philosophy — **structural context first (repo-map), narrow LM output second (unified diff), deterministic host validation third (tree-sitter re-parse)** — is the philosophy MAgHARCM inherits for the 4B–30B SLM regime on per-file-edit tasks. Where [[1.0.0 P-112]] SWE-agent and [[1.0.0 P-115]] OpenHands/CodeAct optimise for *multi-turn repository-issue* resolution, Aider optimises for *single-turn per-file edits*: the repo-map compensates for the SLM's weaker context-tracking, the unified diff compensates for the SLM's weaker free-form generation, and the tree-sitter re-parse compensates for the SLM's weaker self-correction. Every MAgHARCM primitive that touches per-file code editing (PRIM-9, PRIM-22, PRIM-26, PRIM-31) inherits at least one of these three compensations.

## 3. Hop-1 References (papers and systems that Aider cites or builds on)

- [[1.0.0 P-112]] (Yang et al. 2024) — *SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering* (NeurIPS 2024). The canonical tool-calling agent scaffold; Aider's `edit` block is structurally identical to SWE-agent's `edit` ACI. Aider is the **per-file-edit sibling** of SWE-agent's **per-repository-issue** scaffold.
- [[1.0.0 P-113]] (Zhang et al. 2024) — *AutoCodeRover: Autonomous Program Improvement* (ISSTA 2024). The deterministic-retrieval + minimal-diff scaffold; Aider's diff-first output format is the same discipline AutoCodeRover enforces. Aider's repo-map is the **on-demand AST context**; AutoCodeRover's tree-sitter index is the **retrieval-time AST context**.
- [[2.0.0 P-115]] (Wang et al. 2024) — *OpenHands: An Open Platform for AI Software Developers as Generalist Agents* (the CodeAct / OpenHands paper). The third canonical SWE-bench scaffold; cross-evaluated with Aider on the SWE-bench / Aider polyglot split. [INFERENCE: P-115 is the wave-13 OpenHands paper note; if not yet available in the vault when this note is read, treat as a forward reference to be reconciled after the P-115 note lands.]
- Zhang et al. (2023) — *RepoCoder: Repository-Level Code Completion Through Iterative Retrieval and Generation* (arXiv:2303.12570). The flat-RAG predecessor that established the *retrieval-lifts-raw-LM-score* empirical pattern; Aider's chat-loop iterative retrieval is the **interactive generalisation** of RepoCoder's automatic iterative retrieval. RepoCoder is the **hop-1 ancestor** of both AutoCodeRover's automatic retrieval and Aider's chat-driven retrieval. [INFERENCE: candidate slot for P-117 if a dedicated paper note is created; cite as the Zhang et al. 2023 work until then.]
- Cursor / GitHub Copilot / Continue.dev — *companion terminal + IDE coding assistants* (2023–2025). The sibling practitioner tools Aider is routinely compared against in the terminal-coding-assistant literature; Aider's terminal-first philosophy is the contrast point for Cursor's IDE-first philosophy. These systems are **practitioner-anchored** references rather than peer-reviewed papers and are cited as **competitive baselines** rather than intellectual ancestors.
- Anthropic (2024) — *Claude 3.5 Sonnet*. The model that leads the Aider polyglot leaderboard for most of 2024–2025; cited by Aider's maintainer as the "best of breed" for diff-based editing. Aider is the **benchmark harness** through which Claude 3.5 Sonnet's coding capability is publicly demonstrated.
- OpenAI (2024) — *GPT-4o*. The second-place proprietary model on the Aider polyglot leaderboard; Aider's maintainer tracks GPT-4o variants (chat vs "diff-fenced" vs "whole") on the leaderboard as a comparison point.
- DeepSeek-AI (2024) — *DeepSeek-Coder-V2* (MoE, 236B-A21B; arXiv:2406.11936). The **open-weights frontier** that competes with the proprietary frontier on Aider polyglot; cited by Aider as the leading open-weights model and the **canonical SLM/open-weights reference** for diff-based editing.

## 4. Hop-2 References (papers-cited-by-hop-1; one-generation depth)

- Qwen Team (2024) — [[1.0.0 P-21]] / Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct. The open-weights SLM Aider benchmarks alongside DeepSeek-Coder-V2; Qwen2.5-Coder is the **second open-weights frontier** on the Aider polyglot leaderboard and the canonical 7B–32B SLM reference for per-file-edit tasks. Aider's maintainer reports Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct pass-rates in the ~50–70% range depending on size and benchmark edition. [INFERENCE: candidate slot P-58 if referenced.]
- BigCode Project (2024) — [[1.0.0 P-22]] / StarCoder2. The open-weights code-LM lineage Aider benchmarks as the **3B–15B SLM baseline**; StarCoder2 is the historical open-weights ancestor of Qwen2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder. Aider's maintainer tracks StarCoder2 variants as the SLM-floor baseline for diff-based editing.
- Brunsfeld et al. (2013–present) — *tree-sitter: A Parser Generator for Programming Languages*. The concrete-syntax-tree parser library that Aider's repo-map and post-diff re-parse are built on; tree-sitter is the foundational substrate for every structural code retriever in the wave-12 / wave-13 generation. The repo-map is the **AST digest**; the post-diff re-parse is the **recertification** step.
- Myers (1986) — *diff-match-patch algorithm* (the foundational diff library originally published as part of Google's `diff-match-patch` open-source release). The diff algorithm Aider's `unified diff` emission is built on; Aider's host-side diff-application layer uses the same algorithmic lineage. Diff-match-patch is the **per-line, per-character diff primitive** that the agent's "edit = unified diff" output format descends from.
- Robertson, S., Zaragoza, H. (2009) — *The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond*. The foundational sparse-retrieval baseline that Aider's **repo-map-as-context** is contrasted against; Aider explicitly argues that lexical BM25 over chunked text is the wrong substrate for per-file-edit tasks, and that **structural context** (the repo-map) is the right substrate.
- Hendrycks et al. (2021) — *Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding* (MMLU; ICML 2021). The general-capability baseline Aider's maintainer reports alongside the polyglot benchmark; MMLU is the **general-knowledge sanity check** that benchmarks like Aider polyglot are paired with when reporting model capability.
- Karpukhin et al. (2020) — *Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering* (DPR; EMNLP 2020). The dense-retrieval baseline Aider's **structural repo-map** is contrasted against; Aider explicitly argues that dense retrieval over embedded chunks is the wrong substrate for code, and that **structural tree-sitter-derived context** is the right substrate.
- Yao et al. (2022) — *ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models*. The reasoning+acting loop framework that Aider's chat loop instantiates with **chat turns as the action boundary**; each turn is a Thought (the LM's reasoning trace), an Action (`read` or `edit`), and an Observation (the host's response).

## 6. Summary

P-116 Aider (Gauthier 2024–2025) is the **canonical terminal-coding assistant** and **canonical per-file-edit benchmark substrate** for the wave-13 era. Its core contribution — *repo-map (tree-sitter AST digest) + unified-diff output + chat-driven iterative retrieval + post-diff tree-sitter recertification* — is the exact pattern MAgHARCM re-implements in Go with PRIM-9 (CPG), PRIM-22 (DR. JONES comprehension), PRIM-26 (symbol-aware navigator), and PRIM-31 (iterative retrieval refinement) on top. The polyglot benchmark's role as the de facto cross-vendor LLM/SLM coding leaderboard makes Aider the **practitioner evaluation substrate** that complements [[1.0.0 P-111]] SWE-bench (issue resolution) and HumanEval (single-function synthesis). Together with [[1.0.0 P-112]] (SWE-agent, tool-calling), [[1.0.0 P-113]] (AutoCodeRover, structural retrieval), and [[2.0.0 P-115]] (OpenHands/CodeAct, multi-turn agent), P-116 Aider closes the wave-13 evaluation-protocol pillar: a 4B–30B SLM can be scored on per-file edits against Aider polyglot, on repository issues against SWE-bench Verified, and on single functions against HumanEval — three benchmark substrates that bracket the SLM regime's coding capability and provide the calibration data MAgHARCM's per-file-edit primitives are designed against. P-116 is the **practitioner anchor** for everything MAgHARCM builds around per-file code editing in the 4B–30B SLM regime.
